newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton, Yeltsin start talks on upbeat note.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Yeltsin start talks on upbeat note.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin expressed optimism as they sat down for difficult summit talks on Friday, although Yeltsin said he still opposed NATO's plans for enlargement.

The two leaders met in bright sunshine at a secluded modern villa, surrounded by pines and overlooking the partly-frozen Baltic Sea. It is the official residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari, who greeted both men at the door.

Moscow bitterly opposes NATO's plans to take in former Soviet-bloc states in Eastern Europe, saying it would isolate and threaten Russia. Washington says NATO will take in new members as planned and that all Europe will benefit as a result.

Despite some thundering rhetoric from the Kremlin and displays of steely resolve from Washington in advance of the summit, the two leaders seemed upbeat as they prepared to tackle the most difficult questions of European security.
"I think we'll have a good meeting," said Clinton.
"I think both sides are ready to meet each other and, through compromise, to resolve the problems and disagreements," said Yeltsin.
"The sceptics are saying it is impossible to reach agreement on some issues, but we always find a way to negotiate with Bill...Both of the two great powers are duty bound to act in this way."
The Kremlin chief was asked by reporters whether he now accepted the U.S. argument that NATO enlargement, the summit's main focus, posed no threat to Russia.
"I have not been convinced otherwise," he replied.
Nevertheless, Yeltsin said he was confident solutions could be found and that the two men had prepared the ground for Friday's summit at a jovial dinner in Helsinki on Thursday.
"Yesterday, we warmed each other up so that today there won't be such tension at the negotiation," he said.

Clinton, wheelchair-bound because of a leg injury, refused to answer more questions. The two leaders, who have forged a good working relationship in the past and are now meeting for the 11th time, plan a news conference later on Friday.
Clinton arrived first at the villa, flanked by his team of advisers. Yeltsin looked well, although he is clearly still recovering after last year's heart surgery and illness.

Western help for Russia's troubled transition to a market economy and possible deeper cuts in nuclear weapons are also on the agenda. If they can reach agreement, the two sides are expected to issue statements at the end of the summit before Clinton flies back to Washington at 2000 GMT.
Despite the friendly tone, agreement will not be easy once the real business starts -- even though both Clinton and Yeltsin have faith in their post-Cold War partnership.
Yeltsin is under serious pressure from his nationalist and communist critics at home who accuse him, from their stronghold in the Russian parliament (Duma), of selling out to the West.
To make sure the 66-year-old Kremlin chief gets the point and fights Russia's corner, the Duma planned a debate on NATO on Friday which was expected to have a strident anti-Western tone.
Clinton, too, is under pressure on the alliance's expansion.
A NATO summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start membership talks. The new members would not join until 1999 at the earliest.

But those countries, and others in Europe such as the Baltic republics, are watching closely to see there is no backsliding, nor secret deals cut with Moscow over the future of Europe -- as there was in 1945, at the end of World War Two.

U.S. officials said they would also press Russia at the summit to ratify within the next few weeks a long-delayed 1993 arms agreement cutting long-range nuclear missiles, perhaps with the help of additional concessions from Washington.

Yeltsin has just reshuffled his government to bring in more reformers and has drawn lavish praise from Washington on this. There is likely to be more Western help on offer to support Russia as it tackles organised crime and reforms.
